questions.title: What is the "right-to-control theory" that the Supreme Court rejected in Ciminelli v. United States?
questions.question_body: I'm reading United States v. Constantinescu and the court discusses Ciminelli's rejection of the 'right-to-control theory.' The opinion says this theory attempted to 'establish wire fraud by showing that the defendant schemed to deprive a victim of potentially valuable economic information necessary to make discretionary economic decisions.' But I'm confused - isn't the right to control your own assets a property interest? Why did the Supreme Court say this isn't a 'traditional property interest' protected by fraud statutes? And why can't the government base a fraud conviction on depriving someone of information they need to make informed decisions?

questions.title: How does the "fraudulent-inducement theory" differ from the "right-to-control theory" in federal fraud law?
questions.question_body: In Constantinescu, the Fifth Circuit says the indictment properly alleges a 'fraudulent-inducement theory' and distinguishes it from the 'right-to-control theory' rejected in Ciminelli. The court cites Kousisis for the proposition that fraudulent inducement 'is not a repackaging of the right-to-control theory' and that it 'protects money and property.' But I'm struggling to see the practical difference. In both theories, the defendant deceives the victim to get something of value. Why is one valid and the other not? What exactly makes fraudulent inducence different from depriving someone of the ability to make an informed economic decision?

questions.title: Does federal fraud law require proof that the defendant intended to cause economic harm to the victim?
questions.question_body: The defendants in Constantinescu argued that the indictment fails to allege intent to defraud because it only shows they intended to profit - not that they intended to harm their followers. The court cites Kousisis holding that fraud statutes 'do not require a victim to suffer an economic loss' and that a defendant can be liable 'regardless of whether he seeks to leave the victim economically worse off.' This seems counterintuitive to me - I thought fraud required an intent to deceive AND cause harm. If the victims received market-value securities, where's the harm element? How can you have 'intent to defraud' without intent to cause economic injury?

questions.title: What constitutes a "traditional property interest" versus "valuable economic information" under federal fraud statutes?
questions.question_body: Ciminelli says federal fraud statutes protect only 'traditional property interests' and that 'the right to valuable economic information...is not a traditional property interest.' But then the Constantinescu court says inducing followers to purchase securities IS depriving them of a protected property interest (money). I'm confused about where the line is drawn. When I buy a stock, I'm voluntarily parting with money in exchange for something - how is that 'deprivation' of property? And why is depriving someone of 'valuable economic information' (like knowing a stock promoter is secretly selling) not protected, but depriving them of money is? What makes something a 'traditional' property interest?

questions.title: How does 18 U.S.C. § 1348 (securities fraud) relate to mail and wire fraud statutes?
questions.question_body: The court in Constantinescu mentions that § 1348 'borrows key concepts from the mail and wire fraud statutes' and that courts 'have given the terms similar treatment.' I'm trying to understand the relationship between these statutes. Does this mean that when interpreting securities fraud under § 1348, courts should look to mail fraud (§ 1341) and wire fraud (§ 1343) precedent? Why would Congress create a separate securities fraud statute if it essentially mirrors the existing fraud statutes? And what concepts exactly are 'borrowed' - is it just the 'scheme to defraud' language, or something broader?

questions.title: What standard do appellate courts use when reviewing the sufficiency of an indictment?
questions.question_body: The Fifth Circuit in Constantinescu says it reviews 'the sufficiency of an indictment de novo' and must 'take the allegations of the indictment as true.' The court also lays out three requirements: the indictment must '(1) enumerate each prima facie element of the charged offense; (2) fairly inform the defendant of the charges filed against him; and (3) provide the defendant with a double jeopardy defense against future prosecutions.' But I'm confused about the practical application. If the court takes allegations 'as true,' isn't it just rubber-stamping the indictment? At what point does an indictment become insufficient - does it need to include evidentiary details, or just legal conclusions?

questions.title: Why does fraudulently inducing someone to purchase securities count as depriving them of "money or property" under fraud statutes?
questions.question_body: In Constantinescu, the defendants allegedly convinced followers to buy securities through misrepresentations about their trading positions. The court says this sufficiently alleges deprivation of 'money or property' because followers were induced 'to part with their money.' But the followers received the securities they paid for - they weren't outright stolen from. In a typical pump-and-dump, victims buy shares at inflated prices, but they still receive actual shares. How does this constitute 'deprivation' of money or property under fraud statutes? Is the theory that any transaction induced by fraud counts as deprivation, even if the victim receives something in return? And does the victim need to suffer a net loss for there to be 'deprivation'?
